flashcards.q: What are the three current (2026), specific statistics showing the correction away from microservices-by-default?
flashcards.a: CNCF 2025: 42% of orgs actively consolidating microservices back. Gartner: 60% of teams regret microservices adoption for small-to-medium apps (monoliths cut costs ~25% on average). DZone 2024: teams spend 35% more time debugging microservices vs modular monoliths.

flashcards.q: What makes a modular monolith different from an ordinary monolith with a nice folder structure?
flashcards.a: ENFORCED, checkable module boundaries -- a violation is a build/CI failure, not a code-review nit. Mechanisms: language-level privacy (Go unexported, Java JPMS), architecture-test tools (import-linter/ArchUnit), or per-module DB schema separation with no cross-schema joins.

flashcards.q: Name the four defensible reasons to split a monolith into real microservices.
flashcards.a: 1) Independent deployment cadence (a team genuinely blocked by another's unrelated releases). 2) Independent scaling profile. 3) Fault isolation (genuinely different failure modes). 4) Forced polyglot (a proven need for a different language/runtime).

flashcards.q: Mechanically, why does splitting into microservices cost ~35% more debugging time?
flashcards.a: A monolith's request execution is one call stack in one process (grep logs, set a breakpoint). Microservices scatter execution across processes connected by network calls, requiring distributed tracing with correctly-propagated trace context at every hop -- any hop that fails to propagate it leaves a gap exactly where the bug likely is.

flashcards.q: What did Segment's real case study show about consolidating 140+ services back to one application?
flashcards.a: A shared library change required deploying all 140+ services together, defeating the entire purpose of independent deployability -- the services were never truly independent, recreating a 'distributed monolith' with all the operational cost and none of the benefit.

flashcards.q: What did Amazon Prime Video's 2023 case study actually show, and what's the common overstatement?
flashcards.a: One specific monitoring tool moved from serverless/microservices to a monolith, cutting infra cost 90%. Overstatement: treating this as 'Amazon abandoned microservices platform-wide' -- it was scoped to one tool, not the whole Prime Video platform.

flashcards.q: Is monorepo vs polyrepo the same decision as monolith vs microservices? Give the real counter-examples.
flashcards.a: No, orthogonal decisions. Shopify: monorepo + modular monolith. Amazon: polyrepo + microservices. Google: monorepo + many independently-deployed services. The repo-layout choice is about cross-cutting refactor ease (monorepo) vs per-team CI/deploy autonomy (polyrepo).

flashcards.q: How does splitting a monolith's single database into per-service databases change data consistency handling?
flashcards.a: A single-DB transaction (BEGIN/UPDATE/UPDATE/COMMIT, atomic) becomes a saga or outbox pattern across separate databases with eventual consistency -- introducing new failure modes (a lost message between steps causing silent data drift) that literally couldn't occur inside one transactional boundary.

flashcards.q: How does Conway's Law inform where to draw service boundaries, and what happens on a mismatch?
flashcards.a: Architecture tends to mirror organizational communication structure whether designed that way or not -- deliberately draw service boundaries to match team boundaries. A mismatch produces a 'distributed monolith' (teams still coordinating across nominally-independent services) or unnecessary split overhead for coordination that didn't need a network boundary.

flashcards.q: What's the most common mistake teams make when extracting a microservice from a monolith?
flashcards.a: Extracting the code before resolving data ownership -- the new 'service' still reads/writes the monolith's shared database directly, recreating tight coupling through the schema while paying the full network/deployment overhead of separation (the distributed-monolith failure mode).
